notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Acts 13:1–26, drawn from the sources I could access.

---

## Acts 13:1–26 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — The Leadership at Antioch

The church at Antioch (in Syria, where disciples were first called Christians) had five named "prophets and teachers." Ellicott notes that the two roles were not necessarily identical: prophecy implies a more direct message from God by the Holy Spirit, while teaching involves more systematic instruction using reason and reflection.¹ Constable observes that the Greek particle *te* divides the five into two groups: Barnabas, Simeon, and Lucius as prophets; Manaen and Saul as teachers.²

- **Barnabas**: Already known from Acts 4 and 11; a Levite from Cyprus, a "good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith." His name heads the list, suggesting he was the most prominent leader at that point.²
- **Simeon called Niger**: "Niger" is Latin for "black." Ellicott says the name indicates a swarthy African complexion.³ Guzik suggests he was "presumably a black African" and possibly the same Simeon who carried Jesus' cross (Luke 23:26).⁴
- **Lucius of Cyrene**: From North Africa (Cyrene in modern Libya). Likely one of the men of Cyrene who first evangelised Antioch (Acts 11:20). Ellicott notes some have tried to identify him with Luke the Evangelist, but the names Lucius and Lucas are "radically distinct."³
- **Manaen** (BSB: Manaen): Literally "foster-brother of Herod the tetrarch" (Herod Antipas, who beheaded John the Baptist and tried Jesus). Gill traces this name to Menahem, an Essene prophet who foretold Herod the Great's rise and was honoured by him; Manaen may have been the son or grandson, brought up with Antipas.⁵ Guzik notes the striking contrast: two boys raised together — one became a murderer of prophets, the other a prophet and teacher in the church.⁴
- **Saul**: Listed last, reflecting that this list was made before he became the most prominent figure.²

The list shows the cosmopolitan, multi-ethnic character of the Antioch church: a Levite from Cyprus, a black man, a North African, an aristocrat from Herod's court, and a former Pharisee from Tarsus.²

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html (Ellicott)
² https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html (Constable)
³ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html (Ellicott)
⁴ https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/ (Guzik)
⁵ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-13.html (Gill)

### v. 2 — The Holy Spirit's Call

**"As they ministered to the Lord and fasted…"** The Greek verb translated "ministered" is *leitourgein*, used in the LXX and NT for the ministry of priests and Levites in the Temple.¹ Ellicott finds it "probable that a solemn meeting… would end in the 'breaking of bread,' and that, up to that point, those who were so engaged would naturally be fasting."¹ Guzik stresses that "ministering to the Lord" is the first job of any servant of God — worship, praise, prayer — and that they also ministered to the congregation and one another.²

**Fasting**: They "sensed a need to seek God in a special way."² Piper argues that the burden driving them to fast was likely, "Where do we go from here as a church?" — they were seeking the Holy Spirit's leading for the direction of their mission.³ Gill notes that pious Jews fasted twice weekly (Mondays and Thursdays) and that this was likely a special fast, perhaps connected to the famine of Acts 11:28.⁴

**"The Holy Spirit said…"** How? Ellicott believes the Spirit spoke "through the lips of the prophets, speaking as by a sudden burst of simultaneous inspiration" (cf. Acts 20:23).¹ Guzik adds it could have been "simply through the inner witness of the Holy Spirit," quoting G. Campbell Morgan: "I do not for a moment imagine that the assembly heard a voice."² Constable says the mode of communication was less important to Luke than that the Spirit did speak, and that if Luke had specified *how*, every missionary candidate would expect the same type of leading.⁵

**"Separate to Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them"**: The verb implies setting apart for a *new* work. Up to this point they were prophets and teachers in the church; now they receive "a solemn visible mission … consecrating them to the work of the Apostleship to the Gentiles."¹ Gill underlines the theological significance: the Spirit says "to *Me*" — not "to the Lord" or "to God" — demonstrating the Spirit is a divine Person, truly God.⁴ Piper notes that the Holy Spirit had *already* called them (this did not happen in the prayer meeting); now it was simply *time*. God's calling of Saul had been stated as far back as Acts 9:15-16.³

**Reformed note (Piper)**: Fasting expressed hunger for God's leading with the body, not just the heart. "Most of the questions that planning teams have to answer are of that kind" — not explicitly answered in Scripture, needing the Spirit's guidance. The moment of prayer and fasting "changed the course of history," launching a missions movement that would make Christianity the dominant religion of the Roman Empire.³

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
² https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/
³ https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/prayer-fasting-and-the-course-of-history
⁴ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-13.html
⁵ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html

### v. 3 — Fasting, Prayer, and Laying on of Hands

**"After they had fasted and prayed, they laid their hands on them and sent them off."** The repetition of fasting and prayer (already mentioned in v. 2) suggests the fast was prolonged until the laying-on of hands was complete.¹

**Laying on of hands**: This was "a formal commissioning to this work," not bestowing spiritual power but identifying with and encouraging them.² Constable, following I. H. Marshall, says this was "a commissioning for a particular work, not ordination to lifetime service."⁵ Gill is emphatic: this was *not* an ordination — Paul was already ordained as an apostle by Jesus Christ directly (Galatians 1:1), and Barnabas was already an authorised minister. The laying on of hands was a Jewish gesture of blessing and farewell, "wishing them all prosperity and success."⁴

**"They sent them off"**: Guzik highlights that this was historically unprecedented — the first "concerted and organized effort to win people to Jesus," the first time a local congregation intentionally commissioned and sent out missionaries.⁶ Boice notes: "The word 'missionary' has to do with sending. The Latin word *mitto, mittere* means 'to send.'"⁶

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html

### v. 4 — Sent by the Holy Spirit to Seleucia and Cyprus

**"So Barnabas and Saul, sent forth by the Holy Spirit…"** Luke carefully notes that the ultimate sender was the Holy Spirit, not merely the Antioch church (cf. Acts 1:1-2).¹ Ellicott suggests this may refer to a *fresh* revelation guiding them as to the direction of their journey (cf. Acts 16:6-7).²

**Seleucia**: The port city about 15–16 miles west of Antioch, at the mouth of the Orontes River. Built by Seleucus Nicator. They appear to have made no stay there; it was simply the embarkation point.³ Gill notes that ancient sources describe travellers going "down to the sea by Seleucia" to sail to Cyprus.⁴

**Cyprus**: Barnabas's homeland (Acts 4:36).⁵ Constable notes Cyprus was an island of great importance on shipping lanes between Syria, Asia Minor, and Greece. Annexed by Rome in 57 BC, it became a senatorial province in 22 BC governed by a proconsul.⁵

**Sources**:

### v. 5 — Salamis: Preaching in the Synagogues

**Salamis**: The largest town in eastern Cyprus, about 60 miles from Seleucia, with a substantial Jewish population — hence the plural "synagogues." Later renamed Constantia (modern Famagusta).¹ ²

**"They proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues"**: This became Paul's customary pattern — "to the Jew first" (Romans 1:16). The synagogue provided a ready audience of Jews and God-fearing Gentiles who already knew the Scriptures. It was also a practical necessity: if they had begun with Gentiles first, the synagogues would have been closed to them.² Guzik notes that the synagogue service customarily invited any learned man to address the congregation.³

**"John was with them as their helper"**: John Mark (cf. Acts 12:12, 25). Ellicott notes the Greek word for "helper" (*hyperetes*) implies personal service rather than the official "deacon" or "minister." He likely assisted in practical matters and possibly in baptising converts. Gill says he "waited upon them, and provided for them the necessaries of life" — not preaching.⁴ Constable compares him to Timothy on Paul's second journey.²

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-13.html (Gill)
² https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html (Constable)

### vv. 6–7 — Bar-Jesus and Sergius Paulus at Paphos

**Paphos**: At the western extremity of Cyprus, the provincial capital and seat of the Roman governor. Guzik notes it "was infamous for its worship of Venus, the goddess of [sexual] love." Spurgeon is quoted: "Athanasius styled its religion 'the deification of lust.'"¹ Ellicott adds that Paphos was the chief centre of Venus-worship, "conspicuous for the licentiousness of the harlot-priestesses of her temple."²

**Bar-Jesus**: His name means "son of Jesus/Joshua" — a common Jewish name. Gill notes some ancient writers read it as *Barjeus* ("son of counsel"), finding Bar-Jesus inappropriate for a sorcerer.² He was a *magos* (sorcerer/magician) and "false prophet" — a Jew who practised magic, explicitly forbidden in Deuteronomy 18:10-11.³ Constable suggests he may have had Satanic power, like Simon Magus in Acts 8.³

**Sergius Paulus**: A Roman proconsul — the highest official on the island, appointed by the Senate (not the emperor).⁴ Ellicott notes that inscriptions bearing the name "Paulus the Proconsul" have been discovered in Cyprus, confirming Luke's accuracy.⁵ Coins of Cyprus from Claudius's reign also name a proconsul.⁵ Constable reports that "Sir William Ramsay reports that inscriptions bearing Sergius Paulus's name have been found on Cyprus confirming that he was a Christian and that his entire family became Christians."¹

**"A man of intelligence"** (BSB) / "prudent man" (KJV): The Greek *synetos* describes discernment, sagacity. He recognised something in Barnabas and Saul worth investigating and "sought to hear the word of God."⁴

**Sources**:

### v. 8 — Elymas Opposes the Gospel

**"Elymas the sorcerer (for that is what his name means)"**: "Elymas" is the interpretation (not translation) of Bar-Jesus. It derives from an Aramaic/Arabic root meaning "wise man" or "sage" (*ulema*).¹ Gill says his name Bar-Jesus means "son of healing" and Elymas comes from a root meaning "to heal" — he likely posed as a physician or wise counsellor.²

**"Opposed them and tried to turn the proconsul from the faith"**: Bar-Jesus feared losing his influence over the proconsul. Guzik quotes Spurgeon: "Wherever there is likely to be great success, the open door and the opposing adversaries will both be found."¹ Morgan adds: "The severest words of the Bible … are reserved for those who stand between men and truth."³

**Sources**:
¹ https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/
² https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-13.html
³ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html

### v. 9 — Saul, Also Called Paul

**"Then Saul, who was also called Paul…"** This is the pivotal moment where Luke permanently switches to "Paul." Several explanations are offered:

- **Ellicott**: The name change is connected to the conversion of Sergius Paulus. "Paul" was a Roman name, linking him to his illustrious convert — "he was, as it were, claiming a brotherhood with him." The name was similar enough in sound to "Saul" (Saulos/Paulos) to fall within the common practice of dual naming (Jesus/Jason, Silas/Silvanus). Ellicott dismisses the theories that *Saulos* had an opprobrious meaning ("wanton") or that *Paulus* ("little") commended itself to his humility as "more or less fantastic."¹

- **Gill**: Saul was his Jewish name, Paul his Roman name, both given by his parents at birth because he was both a Jew and a Roman citizen of Tarsus. He used Saul among Jews and Paul among Gentiles.²

- **Constable**: "Paul" means "little," perhaps an allusion to physical stature; it rhymes with "Saul" ("asked"). The change at this point in Luke's narrative signals that "Paul's ministry to the Gentiles really began."³

- **Guzik**: Following Lenski, both names were given at birth — his father called him "Saul" while Greek playmates called him "Paul."⁴

- **Longenecker** (cited by Constable): From this point on, Luke always uses "Paul" and (except for situations where Barnabas was more prominent) always lists him first, emphasising his leadership. The conversion of Sergius Paulus was "a turning point in Paul's whole ministry," inaugurating "a new policy in the mission to Gentiles — viz., the legitimacy of a direct approach to and full acceptance of Gentiles apart from any distinctive Jewish stance."³

**"Filled with the Holy Spirit, looked directly at Elymas"**: The Greek implies "a sudden access of spiritual power, showing itself at once in insight into character, righteous indignation, and prevision of the divine chastisement."¹ Guzik notes this was "a fresh filling" (Greek aorist participle) empowering Paul for the confrontation.⁴

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
² https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-13.html
³ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html
⁴ https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

### v. 10 — Paul's Rebuke

**"O child of the devil and enemy of all righteousness…"** Ellicott detects an intentional play on words: his name Bar-Jesus means "son of the Saviour," but in character he is "child of the devil."¹ Paul's language echoes Isaiah 40:4 about making crooked paths straight — Elymas was "perverting the straight ways of the Lord."¹ Constable notes the triple contrast: instead of being full of wisdom, Elymas was full of deceit; instead of being son of a saviour, he was son of the devil; instead of promoting righteousness, he was making God's straight ways crooked.²

**"Full of all kinds of deceit and trickery"** (BSB): The Greek word for "trickery" (*rhadiourgia*) occurs only here in the New Testament. Its primary meaning is "ease in working" which passed through the stages of "versatility," "shiftiness," and "trickery."³

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
² https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html
³ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html

### v. 11 — Temporary Blindness

**"The hand of the Lord is against you… you will be blind… for a time"**: The phrase "hand of the Lord" is an anthropomorphism conveying direct divine chastisement (cf. 1 Kings 18:46; Ezekiel 1:3).¹

Guzik and Ellicott both draw a parallel to Paul's own experience on the Damascus Road: "God gave Elymas a physical blindness that matched his spiritual blindness."² The significant difference: Paul repented; we never hear of Elymas doing so.²

That the blindness was "for a time" (*for a season*) implies it was intended to be remedial, not merely retributive.¹ Ellicott detects "the precision of the trained physician" (Luke) in the description of "mist and darkness" coming over him. The Greek verb tense suggests Elymas "sought and did not find" anyone to lead him — "he had no friends to help him, and was left to his fate unpitied."¹

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
² https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

---

### v. 12 — The Proconsul Believes

**"When the proconsul saw what had happened, he believed, for he was astonished at the teaching about the Lord."** Constable notes simply: "This show of superior power convinced Sergius Paulus of the truth of Paul's gospel, and he believed it. Notice again that belief is all that was necessary for his salvation."¹

Guzik emphasises that Sergius Paulus was astonished "at the teaching of the Lord" — not merely at the miracle, but at the doctrines of God's gracious gift in Jesus through the cross.² Ellicott renders it: "being astonished at the doctrine of the Lord" — the genitive is "of the object, the teaching which had the Lord, i.e., the Lord Jesus, as its main theme."³

Constable notes extrabiblical evidence that Sergius Paulus's daughter and other descendants also became Christians.⁴ Ramsay's archaeological work confirmed this.⁴

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html
² https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/
³ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
⁴ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html

### v. 13 — Perga and John Mark's Departure

**"Paul and his companions"** (BSB: "Paul and his companions"; literally "those about Paul"): Luke's description signals Paul's new position as leader. Previously the group was described as "Barnabas and Saul" (v. 7); now it is "Paul and his party."¹ Guzik notes this shift in leadership is now firmly established.²

**Perga in Pamphylia**: Capital of Pamphylia, about 12 miles inland from the major seaport of Attalia, on the river Cestrus.³ The absence of any record of evangelism there suggests there were no synagogues, and Paul and Barnabas adhered to their plan of preaching to the Jew first.⁴

**"John left them to return to Jerusalem"**: We are not told why. Conjectures include:
- Homesickness (his mother Mary lived in Jerusalem, Acts 12:12)⁴
- Fear of the dangerous journey ahead through bandit-infested Taurus Mountains to Pisidian Antioch (climbing from sea level to 3,600 feet)³
- Resentment that leadership shifted from his cousin Barnabas to Paul²
- Disagreement over the direct approach to Gentiles — Mark had strong Jerusalem church ties⁵
- Paul's poor health (Galatians 4:13 mentions a "weakness of the flesh")²

Paul clearly regarded the departure as unjustified (Acts 15:38 — he "had deserted them"). Yet Mark was later restored to Paul's fellowship (2 Timothy 4:11).²

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
² https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/
³ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html

### vv. 14–15 — The Synagogue at Pisidian Antioch

**Pisidian Antioch**: About 100 miles north of Perga, at 3,600 feet elevation on the slopes of Mount Taurus. One of many cities founded by Seleucus Nicator and named after his father Antiochus. It had a considerable Jewish population and many Gentile proselytes.¹ It was in the region later known as Galatia.²

**"They entered the synagogue on the Sabbath and sat down"**: Sitting was the posture of a teacher (Rabbi). By doing so they indicated they were willing to address the congregation.¹

**The synagogue service**: Opening prayers, then a reading from the Law (the Pentateuch, divided into 53–54 *paraschioth* or sections), then a reading from the Prophets (the *Haphtaroth*). After the readings, any learned visitor could be invited to give an exhortation.¹

**A precise dating**: Ellicott notes two "curious coincidences." Paul's opening words refer to Deuteronomy 1:31 (the lesson for the 44th Sabbath of the year, which fell in July or August), and the corresponding prophetic reading was Isaiah 1:1-27, from which Paul also quotes. "He starts, as was natural, from what the people had just been listening to, as the text of his discourse."¹

**"Brothers, if you have a word of encouragement for the people, please speak"**: The synagogue rulers (lay elders) extended the customary invitation.²

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
² https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

---

### v. 16 — Paul's Opening Gesture and Address

**"Paul stood up, motioned with his hand…"** The gesture was one of commanding silence and attention. Ellicott notes this as a "graphic touch" suggesting an eyewitness source. A similar gesture is recorded in Acts 21:40.¹

**"Men of Israel and you Gentiles who fear God"**: Paul addresses two distinct groups — born Jews ("Men of Israel") and Gentile "God-fearers" (proselytes of the gate who attended synagogue but had not undergone full conversion to Judaism).¹ This dual address frames the entire sermon. Constable notes Paul's sermon follows the pattern of Peter's at Pentecost and Stephen's defence: preparation for Messiah (vv. 16–25), rejection, crucifixion and resurrection of Messiah (vv. 26–37), and application (vv. 38–41).²

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
² https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html

---

### v. 17 — God Chose Israel and Delivered Them from Egypt

**"The God of the people of Israel chose our fathers"**: Paul follows Stephen's model (Acts 7) in beginning with a recapitulation of Israel's history — a theme Israelites never tired of hearing. It demonstrated that the apostles recognised Israel's history as the history of God's chosen people. Paul strategically uses "our fathers," identifying himself with his Jewish hearers.¹

**"He made them into a great people during their stay in Egypt"**: The word for "exalted" (KJV) echoes Isaiah 1:2 ("I have nourished and brought up children") — the very prophetic lesson just read in the synagogue. Israel could only be spoken of as "exalted" in Egypt in the sense of multiplying greatly in population.¹

**"With an uplifted arm He led them out"**: Classic Exodus language emphasising God's mighty, miraculous deliverance.²

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
² https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

---

### v. 18 — Forty Years in the Wilderness

**"He endured their conduct for about forty years in the wilderness"** (BSB): The Greek word translated "endured" (*etropophoresen*) differs by a single letter from one meaning "to nurse, to carry as a father carries his child" (*etrophophoresen*). Some manuscripts have the latter, which recalls Deuteronomy 1:31: "the LORD your God carried you, as a man carries his son." Both readings have strong manuscript support.¹ The BSB ("endured") follows the reading emphasising God's patience with Israel's rebellion; the alternative ("bore them as a nursing father") emphasises God's tender care. Guzik follows the alternative reading, noting that God "put up with their ways" — but the stress is on God's faithful provision despite their unfaithfulness.²

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
² https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

---

### v. 19 — Seven Nations and the Inheritance

**"Having vanquished seven nations in Canaan, He gave their land to His people as an inheritance"**: The "seven nations" refers to the list in Deuteronomy 7:1 (Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites).¹ This is a compressed summary of the conquest under Joshua, emphasising that it was God who destroyed the nations and God who distributed the land — all by His sovereign grace.²

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
² https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

---

### v. 20 — The 450 Years and the Judges

**"All this took about 450 years. After this, God gave them judges until the time of Samuel the prophet."** There is a textual and interpretive question about what the 450 years covers:

- **Constable**: The "about 450 years" probably includes Israel's 400 years in Egypt, the 40 years in the wilderness, and about 10 years of conquest and settlement (approximately 1845–1395 BC).¹

- **Ellicott**: The reading and arrangement are disputed. Some manuscripts place "about 450 years" with the period of the judges (as the BSB does: "After this, God gave them judges… All this took about 450 years"). Others attach it to the previous clauses. The period of the judges from the conquest to Samuel was traditionally reckoned at about 450 years.²

This is one of the more difficult chronological notes in Acts, but Paul's use of "about" (*hos*) indicates an approximate figure, not a precise calendar calculation. Guzik simply notes Paul is giving a broad summary of Israel's history leading to Jesus.³

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html
² https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
³ https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

---

### v. 21 — Saul, Son of Kish

**"Then the people asked for a king, and God gave them forty years under Saul son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin."** Paul mentions King Saul briefly and without elaboration. The forty-year reign is not recorded in the Old Testament (which gives no total for Saul's reign), but Josephus also assigns Saul a forty-year reign.¹ Paul's emphasis falls not on Saul but on David, his successor.

Paul himself was a Benjamite named after this king (Saul/Paul). Guzik suggests Paul may have identified personally with the removal of the first Saul to make way for God's true king.²

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html
² https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

---

### v. 22 — David, a Man after God's Own Heart

**"After removing Saul, He raised up David as their king and testified about him: 'I have found David son of Jesse a man after My own heart; he will carry out My will in its entirety.'"**

This is the theological high point of Paul's historical summary. Constable: "It was particularly David's heart for God resulting in his carrying out God's will that Paul stressed. These qualities marked David's successor, Jesus Christ, too."¹

**R.C. Sproul (Reformed)**: In his sermon on this passage, Sproul explains that God chose David not because David was sinless (he was not), but because David had a heart oriented toward God. David was chosen to be "the ancestor of a greater King, our Lord Jesus Christ." The promise to David was ultimately messianic.²

Guzik notes: Paul's point is that "Christianity is not just a philosophy or a set of ethics… Essentially Christianity is a proclamation of facts that concern what God has done" (quoting Boice). Paul anchors everything in actual events of history leading to Jesus.³

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html
² https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/pauls-sermon-antioch
³ https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

---

### v. 23 — Jesus, the Promised Saviour from David's Line

**"From the descendants of this man, God has brought to Israel the Savior Jesus, as He promised."** This verse is the climax and pivot of the historical summary. Constable identifies the promise as likely Isaiah 11:1-16, which speaks of Messiah coming from David's line.¹ Paul's whole survey — the patriarchs, Egypt, wilderness, conquest, judges, kings — all led here: to Jesus.

Guzik: "This survey of Israel's history demonstrates that God has a plan for history, and we need to sense a connection to that plan. Jesus is the goal of history, and as we are in Jesus, we are in the flow of God's great plan of redemption."²

**Sources**:
¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html
² https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

### vv. 24–25 — John the Baptist's Witness

**"Before the arrival of Jesus, John preached a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel."** John prepared the way. Paul presents John as a witness who pointed away from himself to Jesus — John is not the Saviour; he is the herald.¹

**"Who do you suppose I am? I am not that One… whose sandals I am not worthy to untie"**: Guzik explains the cultural background: rabbis expected disciples to serve them, but it was considered too demeaning to require a disciple to undo the strap of a sandal. John says he is not even worthy to perform this most menial act for Jesus.² Ellicott notes the oldest manuscripts read "What think ye that I am?" rather than "Who."³

John's witness is the perfect bridge from Israel's history to Jesus: John was the last and greatest of the prophets, and he said, "Not me — Him."

### v. 26 — "To Us This Message of Salvation Has Been Sent"

**"Brothers, children of Abraham, and you Gentiles who fear God, it is to us that this message of salvation has been sent."** Paul again addresses both groups, as in v. 16. The Cambridge Greek Testament notes that the oldest manuscripts read "to *us*" (not "to you"), which "is quite in accord with the language of v. 17, 'God chose *our* fathers.' The Apostle through the whole address avoids, as far as may be, wounding any Jewish prejudice and so classes himself with his hearers."¹

Gill explains: "the word of this salvation" means either the Lord Jesus Christ himself, "the essential and eternal *Logos*, or word of God … who is the author of salvation," or more likely the Gospel, which "is not a proposal of terms, by complying with which men may be saved … but it is a declaration of salvation itself, as being a thing done by Christ."²

Constable: "Paul paused to address his hearers by groups again … and to personalize the gospel message to them. He noted that the gospel is for both Jews and Gentiles."³ Guzik: Paul addresses "both Jews and 'near Jews,' those Gentiles who admired the Jewish religion but did not make a full commitment to Judaism."⁴

This verse marks the transition in Paul's sermon from the historical preparation (vv. 17–25) to the proclamation of the gospel events — the rejection, crucifixion, and resurrection of Jesus (vv. 27–31).⁴

## Summary of Tradition-Specific Perspectives

### Reformed (Ligonier / R.C. Sproul)
Sproul emphasises God's sovereign choice of David, not for David's merit but because God purposed to bring the greater King (Christ) through his line. Sproul also highlights the shift in leadership from Barnabas to Paul as providentially ordered. The sermon at Pisidian Antioch is presented as the first recorded Pauline sermon, and Sproul traces how Paul, following Stephen's model, connects all of redemptive history to Jesus.¹

¹ https://learn.ligonier.org/sermons/pauls-sermon-antioch

### Reformed Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper)
Piper focuses on vv. 1–4 and the practice of fasting. He argues that fasting expressed hunger for God's leading and that "this moment of prayer and fasting resulted in a missions movement that would make Christianity the dominant religion of the Roman Empire within two and a half centuries." He stresses that the Holy Spirit had *already* called Barnabas and Saul — the prayer meeting was not about discerning a *new* call but about receiving the timing. God typically reveals His purposes to the leadership of the local church gathered in worship and fasting.¹

¹ https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/prayer-fasting-and-the-course-of-history

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik)
Guzik reads the passage with an emphasis on the Holy Spirit's active, personal guidance — speaking to the church during worship, filling Paul afresh for confrontation, and directing the mission. He draws a parallel between Paul's own blindness and Elymas's (the difference being repentance), and stresses that the church at Antioch launched the first intentional missionary enterprise without "a committee report, without a demographic analysis, without a marketing survey … only with the call and power of the Holy Spirit."¹

¹ https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/acts-13/

### Older Baptist (Gill)
Gill is careful to assert that the laying on of hands in v. 3 was *not* ordination — Paul was already an apostle by direct call of Christ. He sees the Spirit's command "separate to *Me*" as proof of the Spirit's deity and personhood. He provides extensive historical and geographical detail, particularly about Cyprus and the names of the leaders. Gill also interprets "the word of this salvation" (v. 26) as a declaration of salvation already accomplished by Christ, not a proposal of terms.¹

¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/acts-13.html

### Anglican (Ellicott)
Ellicott provides rich historical, lexical, and liturgical insight. He notes the word *leitourgein* (v. 2 — "ministered") is the root of "Liturgy" and likely points to a service culminating in the Lord's Supper. He identifies the precise Sabbath (44th of the year, July/August) from the synagogue lectionary readings. He sees the name change to "Paul" as connected to the conversion of Sergius Paulus, and dismisses speculative etymologies.¹

¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/acts-13.html

### Evangelical / Dallas Seminary (Constable)
Constable emphasises Luke's narrative purpose: to show the legitimacy of the Gentile mission. The blinding of Elymas parallels Peter's confrontation with Simon Magus (Acts 8), validating Paul's apostolic authority. The conversion of Sergius Paulus is "a turning point in Paul's whole ministry," inaugurating a direct Gentile approach. Constable follows Ramsay's archaeological findings that confirm Luke's historical accuracy regarding Sergius Paulus and the proconsular status of Cyprus.¹

¹ https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/acts-13.html
